nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic drifting algae in the clear reef waters. They are the base of the plankton food chain.

nodes.name: Turtle grass
nodes.desc: Seagrass that carpets the sandy lagoon floor behind the reef. Conch, green turtles and manatees graze it.

nodes.name: Reef algae and macroalgae
nodes.desc: Algae growing on reef rock and sand. Grazers such as parrotfish and conch keep it from smothering corals.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: Mangroves fringe the cayes and shoreline. Their leaves are eaten by manatees and their roots shelter young fish.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny crustaceans of the plankton that graze phytoplankton and feed corals and many small animals.

nodes.name: Queen conch
nodes.desc: Large sea snail that grazes algae and seagrass on sandy lagoon floors. It is food for turtles, lobsters, rays and nurse sharks.

nodes.name: Stoplight parrotfish
nodes.desc: Scrapes algae from reef rock with its beak-like teeth and excretes sand. Its grazing helps corals compete with algae.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults graze seagrass and algae. The reserve system protects nesting and feeding areas for green, hawksbill and loggerhead turtles.

nodes.name: West Indian manatee
nodes.desc: Large herbivore of shallow coastal waters that eats seagrass and mangrove leaves. Boat strikes are a growing risk.

nodes.name: Elkhorn coral
nodes.desc: Branching reef-builder of the shallow reef crest. It takes in food from plankton as well as from its algal partners.

nodes.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
nodes.desc: Night-feeding crustacean of reef crevices that eats snails such as conch, other molluscs and small animals.

nodes.name: Nurse shark
nodes.desc: Bottom-feeding shark that eats conch, lobsters and other invertebrates, often resting under reef ledges by day.

nodes.name: Nassau grouper
nodes.desc: Reef predator of fish and crustaceans. It gathers in huge spawning groups each winter, as at Glover's Reef, and is Critically Endangered.

nodes.name: Red lionfish
nodes.desc: Invasive fish that eats small fish and crustaceans on Caribbean reefs and can cut the numbers of native reef fish.

nodes.name: Spotted eagle ray
nodes.desc: Ray that crushes conch and other shelled prey on sandy flats near the reef.

nodes.name: Caribbean reef shark
nodes.desc: Top reef predator of bony fishes and rays. Overfishing has reduced its numbers off Belize.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: Wide-ranging shark with a very broad diet that includes sea turtles and other sharks.

nodes.name: Common bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: Hunts fish in lagoons and along the reef, sometimes herding shoals. Large sharks are its main predators.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Clear shallow water lets light reach the seagrass, algae and coral on the sea floor.

nodes.name: Warm sea temperature
nodes.desc: Corals live in a narrow warm band. Marine heat waves cause bleaching, which hit the Belize reef in 1998.

nodes.name: Nutrients and runoff
nodes.desc: Nutrients from land and recycled from dead matter feed plankton and algae. Excess runoff favours algae over coral.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the water and sediment.
